6.1: The garden was open, and neighbors wanted a story-making station they could share at different places. Inside an unused workshop, Nib unrolled a magnificent plan wider than the door. Lark measured the actual opening. Beside it she drew four requirements: portable, dry, readable, and usable together. The door would keep its present size.

“In unpack and unlock, un changes the action,” Lark modeled clearly. “Pack puts things together for carrying; unpack reverses that. Lock secures something; unlock reverses that. Read the visible base, add un, and check the new whole meaning.”
“Read unpack on the storage note,” Lark invited gently. “Which small existing press can we lay out for one useful design?”

Nib unlocked the correct storage latch. A small hand press and its needed frame parts came onto the supported bench. The enormous drawing remained a drawing. Lark kept the door measurement and four requirements beside the smaller model. Its feed tray faced the wall, giving the next revision a clear purpose.
I can unlock the box. We can unpack the press.
“What do the helpers unpack?” Lark asked gently. “Which action happens to the box first?”
Your first workshop journal page showed the real press, the unchanged door, and four visible jobs the finished station must do. Nib had found a useful beginning among many almost-finished ideas.
6.2: The feed tray pointed neatly into the wall. Nib studied the wall as if a new doorway might solve everything. Lark touched the tray's actual bracket. The workshop could stay where it was. One unloaded part needed fitting again in a better direction.

“Re can mean again in these words,” Lark modeled clearly. “Pack again becomes repack. Fit again becomes refit. Do again becomes redo. Read the base and the added part, then name the small action we actually need to repeat.”
“Read refit on the revision note,” Lark invited warmly. “Which way should the tray face to leave working space?”

Nib released the unloaded tray while Lark supported its weight. It turned on its own bracket and fitted toward the clear bench area. The revision worked without a new workshop. Now the tray could be reached, but a long press handle swept through the place where a second helper needed to stand.
I can refit the tray. We can repack the box.
“Which thing is fitted again?” Lark asked gently. “Which action happens to the box instead?”
Lark drew the revised tray on your journal page. One observed problem had one useful correction. The next test would ask whether two helpers could use the same station together.
6.3: Nib pulled the long handle through a grand sweeping arc. Lark stepped back because it crossed her whole working place. Nib could operate the press, but nobody could help him feed the paper. The four requirement pictures remained beside the model, including the one showing two helpers.

“Help plus ful becomes helpful,” Lark explained clearly. “The ending is weak in ordinary speech, not a separate strongly spoken full. Hopeful works the same way. Read the parts, rejoin the word, and ask whether the object really helps the intended job.”
“Read helpful on our test card,” Lark invited gently. “Which handle leaves the second helper's footprint clear?”

Nib fitted a shorter supported handle. Lark stood in the marked second place while he tested its travel. Neither helper had to jump away. The handle still reached its stop and worked the press. The cooperative requirement had a real test behind it, even though the paper feed still needed attention.
The short handle is helpful. I am hopeful.
“What does the first sentence call helpful?” Lark asked gently. “Which sentence describes a feeling?”
Your journal showed both working places. Nib liked the shorter handle's useful reach. Next, a sheet of paper needed to arrive flat instead of racing past the printing position.
6.4: Nib pulled the paper with a flourish. A corner folded beneath the roller, and the printing space stayed empty. Lark loosened the unloaded feed before the crease grew deeper. The alignment marks were still visible on both sides of the sheet.

“Ly changes how an action is described in slowly and softly,” Lark modeled clearly. “Read slow plus ly, then soft plus ly. The feed note uses those words for an actual job: moving the paper flat. It isn't asking for a race or a timed performance.”
“Read slowly on the feed note,” Lark invited gently. “Which alignment marks keep the sheet flat as it moves?”

Nib held the roller steady while Lark guided the sheet along the visible marks. At a comfortable pace, it reached the print position without a trapped corner. The paper could now arrive where it belonged. Behind it, the rest of the roll stretched across the bench with no clear page ending.
Feed the sheet slowly. Set it softly on the mat.
“How should the sheet move?” Lark asked gently. “Find the describing word in the first sentence.”

Your journal kept a flat-sheet drawing beside the alignment marks. The feed worked without measuring anyone's reaction time. The next question was how much paper would make a page somebody could carry.
6.5: Nib unrolled a magnificent paper path across the workshop. Nobody could lift it without standing on its middle. It was certainly long enough for an impressive story, but not a page for the garden's little reading rest. Lark held the rest's actual outline beside the roll.

“End plus less makes endless: without an end,” Lark modeled clearly. “Hope plus less makes hopeless, a different meaning from hopeful. Listen to the ordinary weak ending, read the parts, and check how less changes the whole word.”
“Read endless on our comparison card,” Lark invited gently. “Which marked length fits the reading rest rather than the whole workshop?”

Nib marked a page boundary against the real outline. The workshop keeper separated the sheet at that mark while everyone else stood clear. The cut page could be lifted and carried without dragging a trail. The remaining roll stayed on its holder for later pages, instead of disappearing after one print.
The page is endless. The sheet can fit the rest.
“Which piece can fit the reading rest?” Lark asked gently. “Which sentence tells us why a sheet is useful?”
Lark drew a real page with four edges in your journal. The station could feed it and a reader could hold it. Now sheets and tools needed labeled storage that made retrieval possible.
6.6: The workshop had several bins, but every label named only one object. Nib put everything that looked numerous into the biggest box. When Lark asked for a clean sheet, a handle arrived first. The station needed labels matched to contents rather than container size.

“Plural endings can have different sounds,” Lark modeled clearly. “Cats ends with /s/, bins with /z/, and boxes with an extra /iz/ syllable. Read the base and ending, then connect the word to more than one of the things it names.”
“Read the storage labels,” Lark invited gently. “Which one belongs to the clean sheets, and which names the tools?”

Nib sorted the supplies into their intended bins. Lark attached the corrected labels, and they tried a real retrieval. A sheet came from the paper place, and a tool came from its own box. Beside them, a painted cover had finished drying over several story days. An older note still described it as waiting.
The cats sit by the bins. I can shut the boxes.
“What can the speaker shut?” Lark asked gently. “Which sentence names the cats?”
Your journal recorded the working storage layout. The next helper could find paper without opening every box. The finished cover needed its old progress note brought up to date.
6.7: The cover was dry. The earlier note still said it was waiting. Nib proposed repainting it to make the scene match the old note. Lark showed the completed-work record instead. A record should follow the actual work, rather than make finished work happen again.

“We already met the different ed sounds,” Lark reminded you warmly. “When hope already ends in e, add d for hoped. Bake becomes baked the same way. Painted keeps its extra ending syllable. Read the visible base and the actual change before rejoining each word.”
“Read the completed-work note,” Lark invited gently. “Does the dry cover need new paint, or does its old label need updating?”

Nib checked the real surface with the keeper. Lark updated the note to painted and dry, leaving its earlier date visible. The cover fitted over the station without a new coat of paint. Underneath, the moving feed belt had a loose side guide that needed checking next.
Sam baked. Pat painted the box.
“Who painted the box?” Lark asked gently. “What completed action belongs to Sam?”
Your journal showed the finished cover on the machine. A more accurate note had saved a needless job. The feed belt could be tested once its loose edge was properly guided.
6.8: The belt moved around its rollers, but one loose side began slipping outward. Nib called it running away. Lark stopped the unloaded mechanism. The belt stayed attached while they studied the side-guide diagram beside the actual roller.

“For these short-vowel bases, double the final consonant before ing,” Lark modeled clearly. “Run becomes running; tap becomes tapping; hop becomes hopping. The doubled letter preserves the spelling pattern. It doesn't add a second consonant sound when we speak the word.”
“Read running on the belt note,” Lark invited gently. “Which guide keeps the moving belt on its own rollers?”

Nib seated the side guide while Lark held the belt level. One slow test movement carried it around the rollers without slipping. They checked its return to the starting point before leaving it fitted. Nib wrote a cheerful note about hoping the next test would work, and its spelling suggested another useful comparison.
The belt is running. Sam is tapping the box.
“What is running?” Lark asked gently. “Which sentence describes Sam's different action?”
Your journal kept running beside the securely guided belt. No hopping was needed beside the mechanism. Nib's next note would need to distinguish that action from the rather different idea of hoping.
6.9: Lark read Nib's note as hopping and began to demonstrate, then caught herself beside the carefully aligned press. Nib pointed to the long-vowel base he had intended. He wanted to describe hoping for success, not bouncing near the rollers.

“Compare hop and hope,” Lark modeled clearly. “Hop doubles p for hopping. Hope drops its final e before ing to make hoping, while the long vowel remains. Make becomes making in the same way. Read the bases before comparing the changed words.”
“Read hoping and hopping,” Lark invited gently. “Which word matches Nib's intended meaning without asking anyone to jump?”

Nib corrected the progress note. Lark reread the whole sentence and understood his meaning. The press stayed still throughout the word comparison. Now the fitted tray, short handle, feed, page supply, and cover could become one portable station rather than separate successes scattered across a bench.
I am hoping. Sam is making a box.
“Who is making something?” Lark asked gently. “Does the first sentence say the speaker is hopping?”
Your journal kept the two spellings with their different meanings. The message was clear. The next test returned to the unchanged door and the original requirement that the station must travel.
6.10: The bench version worked. It was still too wide for the door. Nib considered calling it a splendid indoor invention forever. Lark held the original measuring strip beside the opening. Portable had been one of the four promises from the first day.

“Familiar compounds help us keep the whole purpose in view,” Lark explained warmly. “Read storybook, sunlight, and raincoat by their prepared parts. Then read the requirement pictures together: our story-making station must travel, stay dry, print readably, and let helpers work together.”
“Compare the folding-frame plan with the original measure,” Lark invited gently. “Which arrangement fits the same door while keeping the parts attached?”

Nib folded the frame at its real pivots. Lark checked the attached handle and tray against the measuring strip. The folded station fitted the opening without a changed doorway. They unfolded it on the workshop floor and checked that the working places returned to position. A real authored message was the remaining thing to prepare.
The storybook is dry. The raincoat is on the hook.
“Which object is dry?” Lark asked gently. “Which one hangs on the hook?”
Your journal showed the same station folded and working. The four requirements stayed beside it. Now a blank source sheet waited for something an actual reader would want to know.
6.11: Nib arranged a long row of impressive labels on the blank page. Lark read them and still did not know what the page wanted its reader to do. She moved the labels aside, leaving space for one meaningful sentence chosen by the person making it.

“A sentence tells someone something,” Lark explained warmly. “We begin with a prepared capital, leave spaces between words, and end a statement with a full stop. I can unpack the box is one example, not a message you have to choose. We'll reread your actual words for meaning.”
“Choose, arrange, type, or dictate a message for a real reader,” Lark invited gently. “What should your page tell that person?”

The source strip stayed blank until your chosen words were ready. Lark could supply any unprepared spelling and read it back with you. Nib set a clean sheet beside the ink tray and source-plate holder. The station would print the real message rather than award a prewritten sentence as a prize.
I can unpack the box. The sheet is on the tray.
“What can the speaker do?” Lark asked gently. “How is that different from telling us where the sheet is?”

Your journal kept the actual message source with its spaces and full stop. The example stayed available for support. The next outing would test the station at the garden reading place with your own source, paper, and ink.
6.12: The folded station rolled through the same workshop door. Nib carried its packed supplies to the garden reading place. Lark checked the attached parts when they unfolded the frame. The four requirement pictures came too: portable, dry, readable, and usable together.

“Let's reread the message you actually chose,” Lark invited warmly. “We can help with any word. Then we'll check the four original requirements against what the station does here, rather than how splendid it looked in the first drawing.”
“Use the prepared source and clean sheet,” Lark invited gently. “Which job will each helper take so the page reaches its reader?”

Nib set the visible source plate, paper, and ink in their prepared places. Lark helped operate the press while the source was checked against the new page. Any unclear mark could be revised. The station used real supplies to make a readable copy; it did not duplicate books by magic. The workshop stamp joined your collection.
a word from your own message
I am making a page. The helpful team can read it.
“What is the speaker making?” Lark asked gently. “Which sentence tells us who can read it?”

Lark bound The Workshop of Almost. The shared plans and working press remained available for more pages. Only after that project was finished did Nib notice how quiet the familiar brook sounded beside the garden. Tomorrow's question could wait beside today's finished invention.
